name: Burnt-lime plaster in the Epipalaeolithic and Neolithic Levant
summary: People in the Levant made burnt lime from about 16,000 years ago. Early finds include adhesive, architectural plaster and burial plaster. Later Neolithic communities produced it more widely.
description: Burnt lime first appears in the Levant as a hafting adhesive on microliths at Lagama North VIII in Sinai, in the Geometric Kebaran (about 16,000 cal BP). Among the Natufians, a hearth at Hayonim Cave is interpreted as a place where quicklime was made (about 14,000 cal BP), the architecture at Eynan (Ain Mallaha) included lime-plastered features, and at Nahal Ein Gev II burials of about 12,000 years ago were covered with lime plaster that infrared spectroscopy and soil micromorphology show to be of unprecedented quality. Widespread, large-scale production is considered a development of Pre-Pottery Neolithic B farming societies, beginning about 10,000 years ago.

impact.note: Scored on the general view, not on the cited page: lime plaster and later lime mortar became standard in building across Southwest Asia, the Mediterranean and Europe (reach 2, depth 2) and a long line of plasters, mortars and concretes grew from it (generativity 2); reach is lowered from the lead's 3 because lime was reached separately elsewhere, as in Mesoamerica, and descent beyond western Eurasia is not shown.

date.label: c. 14,050 BCE (c. 16 k cal BP)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Remnants of burnt lime on the backs of microliths at Lagama North VIII in Sinai, interpreted as a hafting adhesive, date to the Geometric Kebaran, about 16,000 cal BP, which is about 14,050 BCE.

evidence.supports: was reported from Lagama North VIII in the Sinai, where remnants of burnt lime were found on the back of trapeze-rectangle microliths and interpreted as an adhesive material for hafting during the Geometric Kebaran (c.16 k cal BP)
evidence.locator: Section 'Prehistoric lime plaster in the southern Levant', first paragraph

date.label: c. 12,050 BCE (c. 14 k cal BP)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: A hearth at Hayonim Cave, dated to the Early Natufian, about 14,000 cal BP (about 12,050 BCE), is interpreted as a combustion feature for making quicklime.

evidence.supports: A hearth interpreted as a combustion feature for quicklime production (Bar-Yosef 1983 ; Kingery et al. 1988 ) was found at Hayonim Cave, dating to the Early Natufian (c. 14 k cal BP)
evidence.locator: Section 'Prehistoric lime plaster in the southern Levant'

date.label: Early Natufian, approximately 13,000–11,600 cal BCE
date.basis: Haklay and Gopher assign Shelter 1 to Early Natufian Layer II. The approximate phase bounds are the regional chronology given by Bocquentin and Noûs.

events.statement: Haklay and Gopher describe a lime-plastered bench in Shelter 1 at Eynan (Ain Mallaha), which they assign to Early Natufian Layer II.
events.caveats: The date is a regional phase range applied to the architectural context. The feature’s function remains debated.

evidence.locator: The Early Natufian architectural remains, fig. 1
evidence.supports: The architectural study describes a plastered bench in Early Natufian Shelter 1 (Layer II) and discusses its debated function.
The authors give a regional Early Natufian date of about 13,000–11,600 cal BCE.

date.label: c. 10,050 BCE (about 12,000 years ago)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Lime plaster covering burials at a Natufian cemetery at Nahal Ein Gev II dates to about 12,000 years ago, about 10,050 BCE.

evidence.supports: Our study analysed lime plaster covering burials at a Natufian cemetery in Nahal Ein Gev II, dating to 12,000 years ago.

date.label: from c. 8050 BCE (about 10,000 years ago)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Widespread production of lime plaster is considered a development of Pre-Pottery Neolithic B farming societies in the Levant, beginning about 10,000 years ago, about 8050 BCE.

evidence.supports: the widespread production of lime plaster are considered a development of farming societies during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB), which took place in the Levant beginning about 10,000 years ago

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Is burnt lime known anywhere before the Geometric Kebaran of the Levant? If not, the origin can be raised to first_known.
Lagama North VIII is placed only at the Levant because the source gives no coordinates; give it its own place in Sinai from Bar-Yosef and Goring-Morris 1977.
The Hayonim hearth is 'interpreted as' a quicklime feature; keep it as an interpretation, not a confirmed kiln.
The scale of Pre-Pottery Neolithic B production ('Ain Ghazal, Yiftahel, Asikli) and its fuel cost are not yet checked against sources.
Site coordinates for Hayonim Cave and Nahal Ein Gev II are recalled and should be checked against an archaeological source.

The laboratory report identifies incompletely calcined lime plaster in Eynan sample 86-1, supplied by the Hebrew University Institute of Archaeology via Ofer Bar-Yosef. Dubreuil proposes that the sampled feature was probably the rim of Early Natufian Shelter 1. The Nanterre archive holds a 1955–1961 field sample catalogue in JP220. The relevant entry and field number linking the sample to Shelter 1 remain unverified.

evidence.locator: pp. 224–225, table 1, sample 86-1 and † footnote, and p. 226, Eynan discussion
evidence.supports: Microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray analysis identify incompletely calcined lime plaster in Eynan sample 86-1 from a bench-like built feature. The authors received it from the Institute of Archaeology at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, courtesy of Ofer Bar-Yosef.
Dubreuil proposes that the sampled feature probably corresponds to the plastered rim described by Perrot for Shelter 1. The comparison supplies no shared specimen number.
The Nanterre archive lists a 1955–1961 excavation sample catalogue in dossier JP220. The finding aid does not identify the corresponding field entry.

evidence.locator: The Early Natufian architectural remains, fig. 1
evidence.supports: The architectural study describes a plastered bench in Early Natufian Shelter 1 (Layer II) and discusses its debated function.

research.note: The paper calls the Lagama North VIII adhesive the earliest evidence for burnt lime in the Levant, but no source opened says whether older burnt lime is known elsewhere, so a first-known claim is not established.
